topic: A step-by-step checklist for auditing crawlability, indexing, duplicate URLs, site speed, mobile, and structured data.
reason: New guide supporting the Technical SEO service page (/seo-services/technical-seo) for the keyword technical seo audit checklist.
body_html:
A technical SEO audit checklist is a step-by-step review of whether search engines can crawl, render, and index your site, and whether pages load fast enough for real visitors. Work through crawlability, indexing, duplicate URLs, site speed, mobile rendering, and structured data, then fix whatever blocks the pages that matter most.

What a technical SEO audit covers

Technical SEO is the plumbing under your content. An audit answers three plain questions: can Google find your pages, can it understand and store them, and do they work well for people once they load. Great content can't help a page Google never reaches.

You don't need a big software budget. Google Search Console is free and shows what Google sees. A crawler such as Screaming Frog, or the site audit tools in Semrush or Ahrefs, shows what a bot finds by following your links. Comparing the two views is where most problems show up.

Before you start: set up your tools

  1. Verify a domain property

    In Search Console, a domain property covers every version of the site (http, https, www, and subdomains) in one place, so nothing hides in a version you forgot to add.

  2. List your money pages

    Write down the short list of URLs that bring in leads, sales, or calls. Every issue you find gets checked against this list first.

  3. Run a full crawl

    If your pages rely on JavaScript to show content, turn on JavaScript rendering in your crawler so you see what Google sees.

  4. Note who can change what

    Templates, server settings, redirects, and robots.txt often sit with different people. Knowing the owner up front saves weeks later.

Technical SEO audit checklist, part 1: crawlability

Crawlability means a search engine's bot can reach a page by following links and isn't told to stay away. Tick these off as you go; your progress is saved in this browser.

  • robots.txt doesn't block important folders, or the CSS and JavaScript files pages need to display
  • No internal links point to 4xx pages (fix the link at the source, don't lean on redirects forever)
  • No redirect chains or loops; internal links point straight at the final URL, with 301s for permanent moves
  • No orphan pages: compare the crawl against your XML sitemap and top GA4 landing pages
  • Money pages are reachable within a few clicks of the homepage
  • No 5xx errors in the crawl or in Search Console's Crawl Stats report (Settings, then Crawl stats)

Watch out robots.txt controls crawling, not indexing. Google's introduction to robots.txt says it is not a way to keep a page out of Google; a blocked page can still be indexed if other pages link to it. To keep a page out, use noindex (and let Google crawl the page so it can see the tag) or password protection.

Part 2: indexing

Indexing is Google storing a page so it can appear in search results. Open the Page indexing report in Search Console. Google says not to expect every URL to be indexed, so the question isn't "why are 400 pages excluded" but "are my money pages indexed". Filter the reasons, then use this table to decide what deserves your time.

Status in the reportWhat it meansAct when
Crawled - currently not indexedGoogle fetched the page and chose not to index itIt's a money page: inspect it, then strengthen content and internal links
Discovered - currently not indexedGoogle knows the URL but hasn't crawled it yetIt lingers on important pages: make sure they're linked and in the sitemap
Duplicate, Google chose different canonical than userGoogle disagrees with your canonical tagAlways worth a look: compare both URLs in URL Inspection
URL marked 'noindex'A noindex tag or header is on the pageThe page should rank: remove it and request indexing
Soft 404The page says "not found" but returns a success codeReturn a real 404 or 410, or give the page real content
Page with redirect / Alternate page with proper canonical tagWorking as intendedUsually no action

A few more indexing checks:

  • Stray noindex tags. These often slip in during a redesign, or when a "hide from search engines" setting is left on after launch.
  • URL Inspection on key URLs. It shows whether a page is indexed, which canonical Google chose, and a screenshot of how Google rendered it.
  • Your XML sitemap. List only canonical, indexable pages that return a 200 status. Google's sitemap guidelines say Google ignores the priority and changefreq fields and uses lastmod only when it's consistently accurate.

50,000Max URLs per sitemap file (Google Search Central)

50 MBMax uncompressed sitemap size (Google Search Central)

Part 3: duplicate URLs and canonical tags

The same content often lives at several addresses: http and https, www and non-www, with and without a trailing slash, or with tracking parameters. A canonical is the version you want Google to treat as the main one.

  • One preferred domain version; the others 301 redirect to it
  • Each indexable page has a self-referencing canonical with an absolute URL
  • Canonicals point to live, indexable pages, not redirects or noindexed pages
  • Sitemap, canonical tags, and internal links all name the same URL

Google's canonicalization guide treats redirects and rel="canonical" as strong signals and sitemap inclusion as a weaker one. It also warns against using robots.txt or noindex to choose a canonical.

Part 4: site speed and Core Web Vitals

Core Web Vitals are Google's three measures of real-world page experience: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP, loading), Interaction to Next Paint (INP, responsiveness), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS, visual stability). A page passes when it meets all three "good" thresholds at the 75th percentile of visits.

2.5 sLCP "good" limit (web.dev)

200 msINP "good" limit (web.dev)

0.1CLS "good" limit (web.dev)

  1. Start with the Core Web Vitals report in Search Console. It uses real Chrome user data and groups similar URLs, so one template fix can clear many pages.
  2. Run PageSpeed Insights or Lighthouse on one URL per template (home, service, product, blog), not on every page.
  3. Common fixes: compress and correctly size images, set width and height on images and embeds to stop layout shifts, defer JavaScript that isn't needed right away, and trim third-party scripts you no longer use.

For a deeper walkthrough, see my guide on improving site speed and Core Web Vitals.

Part 5: mobile, rendering, and HTTPS

  • Mobile pages carry the same main content, headings, and links as desktop (Google crawls and indexes the mobile version)
  • JavaScript-loaded content appears in the rendered HTML in URL Inspection
  • Every page is served over HTTPS, http redirects to https, and there's no mixed content

Part 6: structured data

Structured data is code that labels what a page is about, such as a business, product, or article, using the Schema.org vocabulary. Test key pages with Google's Rich Results Test, fix errors, and make sure the markup matches what's visible on the page.

How to prioritize what you find

An audit can surface hundreds of issues. My rule: rank every issue by how many money pages it touches, not by how alarming the tool's label sounds.

PriorityIssue typeWhy
1Money pages blocked, noindexed, or not indexedNothing else matters until these can rank
2Site-wide template problemsOne fix repairs many pages
3Core Web Vitals on your highest-traffic templatesAffects the most real visitors
4Cleanup: old redirects, minor duplicate titlesReal, but rarely urgent

Track each issue in a spreadsheet with the affected URLs, the fix, the owner, and the date fixed. Once fixed, click Validate fix on that issue in the Page indexing report. Google says validation typically takes up to about two weeks and stops if even one affected URL remains, so fix every instance first.

How often should you run a technical SEO audit?

A full audit once or twice a year works for most small and mid-size sites, with a lighter monthly check of Search Console for new indexing errors, Core Web Vitals changes, and crawl problems. Always run one before and after a redesign, platform move, or domain change, since those are the moments when redirects break, noindex tags get left behind, and pages quietly drop out of the index.

Can you do a technical SEO audit yourself?

Yes, for the basics. Search Console, PageSpeed Insights, and a crawler will surface most crawl, indexing, and speed issues on a small site, and this checklist gives you the order to work in. Where it gets harder is diagnosing why a problem happens and fixing it safely, especially redirects, JavaScript rendering, and server settings. That's usually the point where a developer or SEO specialist saves time.

What's the difference between a technical SEO audit and a full SEO audit?

A technical SEO audit looks at the site's infrastructure: crawling, indexing, speed, mobile, security, and structured data. A full SEO audit adds content quality, keyword targeting, on-page optimization, backlinks, and competitors. Many people start with the technical side because content and link work only pays off once search engines can reach and index the pages you're improving.

Get help with your technical SEO

If you'd rather hand this off, I offer a standalone technical SEO audit with a prioritized fix list, and ongoing technical SEO services if you want help putting the fixes in place.

title: Mobile-First Indexing Checklist: Fixing Mobile SEO Issues
seo_title: Mobile SEO Checklist for Mobile-First Indexing
meta_description: Use this mobile SEO checklist to match mobile and desktop content, fix speed and pop-up issues, and test pages the way Google's smartphone bot sees them.
excerpt: Google indexes the mobile version of your site. This mobile SEO checklist covers content parity, metadata, speed, pop-ups, and how to test without the retired Mobile-Friendly Test.
tags: mobile SEO, mobile-first indexing, Core Web Vitals, technical SEO
topic: A checklist for finding and fixing mobile SEO issues now that Google indexes the mobile version of every site.
reason: New post supporting the Mobile SEO service page (/seo-services/mobile-seo) for the keyword mobile seo checklist.
body_html:
A mobile SEO checklist makes sure the mobile version of your site, which Google uses to crawl and index it, has the same content, links, and metadata as desktop, loads quickly on a phone, and is easy to use with a thumb. Here's what to check and how to fix common problems.

Why the mobile version is the one that counts

Google finished its move to mobile-first indexing in October 2023. In plain terms, Google crawls your site with a smartphone bot and builds its index from what that bot sees. If something exists on desktop but not on mobile, Google may not see it at all.

The testing tools changed too. Google retired the Mobile-Friendly Test and the Mobile Usability report in Search Console in December 2023, as announced on the Search Central blog, and pointed people to Lighthouse instead. Many older checklists still tell you to run the retired tool, so here's what to use now.

You want to checkUse now
Speed and usability on a phoneLighthouse in Chrome DevTools (mobile mode) or PageSpeed Insights
What Google's smartphone bot actually rendersURL Inspection live test in Search Console (screenshot and rendered HTML)
Real-user speed by deviceCore Web Vitals report in Search Console (mobile and desktop shown separately)
Content parity across the whole siteTwo crawls, one with a smartphone user agent and one with desktop

Which mobile setup do you have?

How much of this checklist applies depends on how your site serves phones. Google's mobile site and mobile-first indexing best practices describe three setups.

Responsive

  • One URL and the same HTML for every screen
  • Content and metadata match by default
  • Google recommends it as easiest to maintain
  • Focus on layout, speed, and pop-ups

Dynamic serving

  • One URL, different HTML per device
  • Should send the Vary: user-agent header
  • Parity can drift: compare both versions
  • Check robots meta tags on the mobile HTML

Separate URLs (m-dot)

  • A different address, often m.yoursite.com
  • Needs canonical and alternate tags
  • Verify both versions in Search Console
  • Most places for mistakes

My decision rule: if your site is responsive, the parity items below rarely fail, so spend most of your time on speed and pop-ups. If it uses dynamic serving or m-dot URLs, start with parity, because that's where pages quietly drop out of the index.

The mobile SEO checklist

Tick items off as you go; your progress is saved in this browser.

Content and links

  • Main text and headings match desktop (tabs and accordions are fine if the content is in the page)
  • Primary content doesn't load only after a tap, swipe, or typing, since Google's bot won't take those actions
  • Mobile menus still link to important category and service pages
  • Images use the same URLs and alt text as desktop, and aren't too small or low resolution

Metadata and structured data

  • Title tags and meta descriptions match desktop
  • Robots meta tags match desktop, with no mobile-only noindex or nofollow
  • The same structured data appears on mobile pages, with mobile URLs inside it on m-dot sites
  • robots.txt doesn't block CSS, JavaScript, or images the mobile pages need

Layout and usability

  • A viewport meta tag is set to the device width
  • Nothing scrolls sideways, and text is readable without pinching to zoom
  • Buttons and links are big enough, and far enough apart, to tap accurately
  • No full-screen pop-up covers the content right after someone lands

Watch out A noindex or nofollow that appears only on mobile can drop pages from search, because the mobile version is the one Google indexes. This often comes from a plugin or theme setting that serves different code to phones. Check the robots meta tag in the URL Inspection rendered HTML, not just in your desktop browser.

Speed on a phone

Core Web Vitals are Google's measures of loading (LCP), responsiveness (INP), and visual stability (CLS). Here are the "good" marks:

2.5 sLCP "good" limit (web.dev)

200 msINP "good" limit (web.dev)

0.1CLS "good" limit (web.dev)

Mobile is usually the weaker of the two in the Core Web Vitals report. Oversized images, heavy sliders, and stacks of third-party scripts are the usual culprits. My page speed optimization work starts there.

On pop-ups, Google's guidance on intrusive interstitials and dialogs calls out full-screen dialogs that cover the content, such as newsletter or app-install prompts. Small banners that take up a fraction of the screen are fine, and legally required ones, such as an age gate, are treated differently.

How to find mobile SEO issues on your site

  1. Run a URL Inspection live test

    Test your homepage and one page per template. If the screenshot looks broken or blank, check for blocked CSS or JavaScript first.

  2. Run Lighthouse in mobile mode

    Use Chrome DevTools or PageSpeed Insights on the same URLs for speed and usability checks.

  3. Compare two crawls

    Crawl once with a smartphone user agent and once with desktop, then compare word counts, titles, links, and structured data. Big gaps point to parity problems.

  4. Use your own phone

    Tap through your top pages and forms on cellular data, not office wifi. Many problems are obvious in thirty seconds.

Is mobile-first indexing the same as being mobile-friendly?

No. Mobile-first indexing is about which version of your site Google reads: the mobile one. Mobile-friendliness is about whether people can comfortably use that version. A site can be indexed mobile-first and still frustrate visitors with tiny text or pop-ups. A good mobile SEO checklist covers both: content parity for indexing, and layout, speed, and usability for the people who land on the page.

Does Google still have a mobile-friendly test?

Not as a standalone tool. Google retired the Mobile-Friendly Test and the Mobile Usability report in December 2023. For the same kinds of checks, use Lighthouse in Chrome or PageSpeed Insights for speed and usability, and the URL Inspection tool in Search Console to see the mobile page Google renders. Core Web Vitals data by device is still in Search Console.

Do you need responsive design for mobile SEO?

It isn't required, but Google recommends it. Responsive design uses one URL and one set of HTML for every screen size, so there's no risk of the mobile version falling out of sync with desktop. Separate mobile sites can still rank, but they need careful canonical tags, matching content, and matching robots rules, which adds ongoing work and more places for mistakes.

Get help with mobile SEO

If your mobile pages are slow, missing content, or just hard to use, I can help through my mobile SEO services, from finding parity gaps to fixing speed issues on your key templates.

title: What Is a Full-Stack Marketing Agency, and When Should You Hire One?
seo_title: Full-Stack Marketing Agency: What It Is and When to Hire
meta_description: What a full-stack marketing agency does, how it compares to a specialist, when to hire one, and the questions to ask before you sign.
excerpt: A full-stack marketing agency runs strategy, SEO, ads, content, web and reporting as one coordinated plan. Here's when that model fits and what to ask first.
tags: full-stack marketing, digital marketing agency, white label, hiring an agency
topic: What a full-stack marketing agency is, how it differs from a specialist, and when to hire one
reason: Supports the full-stack digital marketing page by answering the definition and hiring question for business owners and agencies.
body_html:
A full-stack marketing agency is one team that handles most or all of your digital marketing: strategy, SEO, paid ads, content, social media, website work and reporting. You should consider hiring one when you need several channels working together and don't have the in-house team to coordinate them.

The term borrows from software, where a "full-stack" developer works on every layer of an app. In marketing, it means the agency covers every layer of how people find, judge and choose you, instead of handling one channel and leaving the rest to someone else.

What does a full-stack marketing agency do?

Service lists vary, but a full-stack setup usually covers these six areas.

Strategy and planning

Goals, audience, budget split across channels and a calendar that ties it together.

Organic search

Technical SEO, on-page work, content and local SEO, including Google Business Profile.

Paid media

Search, display, shopping, video and paid social campaigns.

Content and social

Blog posts, landing page copy, social content and community management.

Website

Design, development, speed and conversion rate optimization (getting more of your existing visitors to take action).

Analytics and reporting

Tracking in GA4 and Search Console, plus one report that shows how channels work together.

The real difference isn't the length of the list. It's coordination. When the same team runs your ads and your SEO, they can use paid search data to choose organic topics, point campaigns at landing pages built to convert and report on everything with one set of definitions.

Full-stack agency vs. specialist agency

Neither model is better in every case. It depends on what you need right now.

Full-stack agency

  • Best for several channels that need to work together
  • The agency handles coordination
  • One combined report
  • Depth varies by service, so ask who does each one

Specialist agency

  • Best for one channel that needs deep focus
  • You handle coordination across vendors
  • Separate reports per vendor
  • Usually deep in its one area

A common middle path is a full-stack agency for day-to-day marketing plus a specialist for one complex project, such as a large site migration.

When should you hire a full-stack marketing agency?

Four situations come up most: you're juggling several vendors, you have no in-house marketing team, your reports don't agree with each other, or you're launching something that touches every channel at once. Run through this quick self-check.

  • Do you currently use three or more separate marketing vendors or freelancers?
  • Is marketing handled by an owner or office manager on top of another job?
  • Do different vendors report different lead or sales numbers for the same period?
  • Are you launching a new website, location or product in the next six months?
  • Can your budget support at least two channels at once?

A full-stack agency is worth a serious look. Use the questions below to compare a shortlist, and ask each one for a sample combined report.

It could go either way. Start with the one or two channels that matter most, and choose a partner who can add more later without changing your tracking.

A specialist is probably the better fit for now. Revisit this if you add vendors or channels.

The vendor problem is the easiest one to underestimate. With one freelancer on social, another on ads and a web developer you call when something breaks, you're the one stitching it together, and gaps appear between them: ads sending traffic to a page nobody optimized, or a site update that breaks tracking. For a small business here in the Capital Region with an office manager running marketing on the side, that coordination time adds up fast.

When a full-stack agency may not be the right fit

  • You only need one channel, and you need it done at a high level.
  • You already have a strong in-house team that needs specialist support in one area.
  • Your budget can't support several channels yet. Doing one or two well usually beats doing six thinly.

What to ask before you hire one

Copy these into an email to each agency on your shortlist. Comparing written answers side by side is easier than comparing sales calls.

1. Which services do you do in-house, and which go to partners?
2. Who is my main contact, and who does the day-to-day work?
3. Can you show a real example of how your SEO, paid and content
   people shared information on one account?
4. Will my ad accounts, GA4, Search Console, Google Business Profile
   and website stay in my name, with your team added as users?
5. Can I see a sample report, and how often will I get one?
6. How do you measure success: leads, sales, revenue or something else?
7. What does early progress look like for each channel you'd run?

Tip Keep ownership of every account. In GA4, keep the Administrator role yourself and give the agency Editor, which per Google's GA4 roles guide controls property settings but can't manage users. For ads, Google explains that a Google Ads manager account lets an agency oversee several client accounts from one sign-in, so it can work in your account without owning it.

Be wary of anyone who guarantees rankings or results. Leads, sales and revenue matter more than impressions.

Can agencies use a white label full-stack partner?

Yes. Some agencies offer full-stack marketing by partnering with a white label team behind the scenes. The agency keeps the client relationship and brand, while the partner delivers some or all of the channels. This lets a design studio or single-channel shop offer a complete package without hiring for every skill. Growthopedia's white label full-stack digital marketing service is built for this.

Is a full-stack marketing agency more expensive?

Not necessarily. Pricing depends on how many channels you use and how much work each one needs. Compared with hiring several separate vendors, a single agency can reduce overlap and the time you spend coordinating. Compared with one specialist, it will usually be a bigger monthly commitment because it covers more. Ask for pricing broken down by service so you can see where the budget goes.

Do I need every service a full-stack agency offers?

No. A good full-stack agency should recommend the channels that fit your goals and budget, not sell you everything at once. Many businesses start with a core mix, such as SEO, Google Business Profile and a focused paid search campaign, then add content, social or conversion work once the basics are producing results. The benefit is that new channels slot into the same plan and reporting.

How long before I see results?

It varies by channel. Paid campaigns can start sending traffic soon after launch, while SEO and content usually take longer to build. Google's guide Do you need an SEO? says no one can guarantee a #1 ranking, so be cautious of fixed promises. Ask any agency to explain what early progress looks like for each channel and how they'll report on it.

One plan for the whole stack

If you're an agency that wants to offer more without hiring for every channel, take a look at full-stack digital marketing for agencies. If you're a business owner, the full list of Growthopedia services shows what can be handled under one plan, along with reporting and analytics that ties it together.

title: Product Listing Ads Explained: Setup, Feeds and Optimization
seo_title: Product Listing Ads: Setup, Feeds and Optimization
meta_description: Product listing ads (Google Shopping ads) explained: how to set up Merchant Center, build a product feed that gets approved, and optimize for profit.
excerpt: Product listing ads run on your product feed, not keywords. Here's how to set them up in Merchant Center and Google Ads, what your feed needs, and how to optimize once they're live.
tags: Google Shopping ads, Merchant Center, product feeds, Performance Max, ecommerce PPC
topic: How product listing ads (Google Shopping ads) work, how to set them up, what the feed needs, and how to optimize them.
reason: New guide to support the /ppc-marketing/product-listing-advertising service page for the keyword "product listing ads".
body_html:
Product listing ads are the image-led product ads that show a photo, price and store name right in Google results. Google now calls them Shopping ads. They run from your product feed in Google Merchant Center, not from keywords, so the quality of your feed largely decides where and how often they appear.

What product listing ads are

"Product listing ads" (PLAs) is the original name for what Google Ads now labels Shopping ads. The old term still describes the format well: each ad is a listing for one product, built from data you send to Google.

Instead of writing headlines and choosing keywords, you give Google a structured product feed. Google reads your titles, descriptions, prices, images and identifiers, then decides which searches each product is relevant for. Better catalog data means better matching.

Your products can also appear for free. Google Merchant Center lets eligible products show in free listings across Google surfaces such as Search, the Shopping tab, Images and Lens. Paid Shopping ads sit on top of that, giving you more placements and more control.

How product listing ads work in Google Ads today

There are two moving parts: Merchant Center, which holds your product data, and Google Ads, which holds your budget and bidding. You link the two accounts, then choose a campaign type.

Standard Shopping

  • Runs only Shopping ads from your feed.
  • You control product groups, bids and campaign priority (which campaign's budget is used when products overlap).
  • Search terms are visible, and you can add negative keywords.
  • Pick it when you need to learn which products and searches actually make money.

Performance Max

  • Uses the same product data but can serve across more of Google, including Search, YouTube and Discover.
  • Hands more targeting and bidding decisions to Google's automation.
  • Any campaign you create inside Merchant Center is a Performance Max campaign.
  • Pick it when conversion tracking is solid and you want reach more than line-by-line control.

My rule of thumb: if you can't yet say which ten products bring in most of your profit, start with Standard Shopping. You'll get clearer data to judge Performance Max against later. If you already know your winners and your conversion values are accurate, testing Performance Max makes more sense.

How to set up product listing ads, step by step

The order matters. Launch before the feed is clean and you spend the first weeks fixing disapprovals instead of learning what sells.

  1. Create and verify Merchant Center

    Add your business details, verify and claim your website, and set up shipping and return policies. Google uses these to judge whether your store is trustworthy.

  2. Add your products

    Connect a platform such as Shopify or WooCommerce, upload a spreadsheet, or use a scheduled feed file. A platform connection keeps prices and stock levels in sync automatically, which prevents many disapprovals.

  3. Fix diagnostics before launch

    Merchant Center flags missing attributes, price mismatches and policy problems. Clear the errors first, then work through the warnings.

  4. Link Google Ads

    Send a link request to your Google Ads account from Merchant Center, then approve it in Google Ads. Billing must be set up in Google Ads before ads can run.

  5. Create the campaign

    Google's Shopping campaign setup guide walks through choosing the Merchant Center account, budget, bidding, priority and product groups. You can't change the linked Merchant Center account after the campaign is created, so double-check it.

  6. Set up conversion tracking

    Track purchases with revenue values in Google Ads, and check them against GA4. Automated bidding is only as good as the conversion data you give it.

What a product feed needs

Google's product data specification lists every attribute. These are the essentials, and what I check first in each:

AttributeRuleWhat to check
idUnique per product, up to 50 charactersIDs stay the same when you update data (Google asks for this), even after a platform switch
titleUp to 150 charactersLeads with searched words, not internal SKU names
descriptionUp to 5,000 charactersDescribes the product itself, not store-wide promotions
linkThe product's landing pageOpens the exact variant, not a category page
image_linkMain product imageClean product shot, no overlays or watermarks
price and availabilityMust match the landing pageSale prices and stock update in the feed when they change on the site

Depending on what you sell, you also need identifiers. Brand is required for most new products. GTIN (the barcode number, such as a UPC) is strongly recommended when your product has one, and Google notes that incorrect or missing GTINs can lead to disapprovals. If a product has no manufacturer GTIN, you supply an MPN instead. Condition is required for used or refurbished items.

Optional attributes like product type, Google product category and custom labels don't get you approved, but they make the campaign far easier to organize later.

Watch out The most common self-inflicted disapproval is a price mismatch during a sale. If you change prices on the site but your feed only updates once a day, the ad and the page disagree until the next fetch. Before a sale, confirm how often your feed refreshes, or schedule the price change to line up with it.

How to optimize product listing ads

Once products are live, most gains come from the feed, the structure and the landing pages, roughly in that order.

Write titles for shoppers, not for your warehouse

Your title does the work keywords do in a text ad. Lead with the words people actually search: brand, product type, and the details that matter for that category. Check the search terms report regularly and fold the language people use back into titles. A simple pattern to adapt per category:

Apparel:      Brand + Product type + Gender + Material + Color + Size
Hardware:     Brand + Product type + Model number + Key spec (size, power)
Home goods:   Brand + Product type + Material + Dimensions + Color
Example:      Women's Merino Wool Crew Sweater, Navy, Medium

Keep the feed title consistent with the product name on the page itself. Google's specification asks titles to accurately describe the product and match the title on your landing page, so a keyword-stuffed feed title that the page doesn't back up is a mistake, not a shortcut.

Use images that sell

The image is the first thing a shopper sees. Use a clean, well-lit main image of the product itself. Merchant Center has image rules (no promotional overlays or watermarks on the main image, for example), so follow them, and add extra images with the additional image attribute.

Structure campaigns around margin and performance

In Standard Shopping, product groups let you split products by brand, category, product type or custom label, then bid differently for each. Custom labels are useful for grouping by margin, season or best sellers. In Performance Max, the equivalent is splitting products across asset groups or campaigns so your best and worst performers don't share one budget.

Before you set any bid, work out what a click is worth to you. The most you can pay per click and still break even is your price, times your margin, times your conversion rate. Use your own numbers here; the defaults are only an example.

Average order value ($)

Gross margin (%)

Conversion rate from Shopping clicks (%)

Break-even cost per click: about ${}

The same math gives you a break-even ROAS (return on ad spend): divide 100 by your margin percentage. At a 40% margin, that's 2.5, meaning every $1 of ad spend has to bring in $2.50 in revenue just to cover product costs. A healthy-looking ROAS can still lose money on low-margin products, so review product groups monthly and shift budget toward what earns. Clear PPC reporting makes this much faster than digging through the platform.

Add negative keywords where you can

Because Shopping ads match from your feed, they can show for loosely related searches. Review search terms and add negatives in Standard Shopping to stop paying for clicks that will never convert.

Send clicks to a page that closes

The ad gets the click; the product page gets the sale. Make sure the page loads quickly, shows the same price and stock status as the ad, and makes adding to cart obvious on a phone. If your product pages need work, my eCommerce SEO services cover the same pages and help both your paid and organic results.

Are product listing ads right for your business?

They usually fit if you sell physical products online, have a reasonable number of them, and can keep product data accurate. They are a weaker fit if you sell services, custom quotes, or products Google restricts in Shopping. Check Google's Shopping ads policies before you invest time in a feed.

Next steps

If you'd like help building a cleaner feed or a campaign structure you can actually read, I offer product listing advertising management for online stores. Send a note whenever you're ready to talk it through.

Is "product listing ads" the same as Google Shopping ads?

Yes. Product listing ads is the older name for the format, and Google Ads now calls them Shopping ads. The mechanics are the same: you send product data through Merchant Center, Google matches products to searches, and the ad shows an image, title, price and store name. You'll still see "PLA" used in agency reports and job descriptions, so it's worth knowing both terms refer to the same thing.

Do I need a website to run Shopping ads?

For standard Shopping ads, yes. Each product needs a landing page where a shopper can see the product and buy it, and Google checks that the price and availability on that page match your feed. You also verify and claim your website in Merchant Center. If you don't have an online store yet, building one with clear product pages is the first step.

Should I use Standard Shopping or Performance Max?

It depends on how much control you want. Standard Shopping runs only Shopping ads and lets you manage product groups, bids and campaign priority directly. Performance Max uses the same feed but serves across more of Google and relies more on automation. Many stores start with one, give it enough conversion data to learn, then test the other against it rather than switching back and forth.

Why are my products disapproved in Merchant Center?

The most common reasons are a price or availability mismatch between your feed and landing page, missing or incorrect identifiers such as GTIN or brand, image problems, and policy issues. Merchant Center's diagnostics show the reason for each product. Fix errors at the source, usually your store platform, so the problem doesn't come back with the next feed update, then request a review if needed.

title: Generative Engine Optimization Strategy: A Step-by-Step Guide
meta_description: Build a generative engine optimization strategy step by step: crawler access, answer-first content, structure, off-site signals and measuring AI citations.
excerpt: A step-by-step generative engine optimization strategy: open the right crawlers, put answers first, structure passages, build off-site trust and track AI citations.
tags: GEO strategy, AI Overviews, AI Mode, ChatGPT search, AI visibility
topic: A step-by-step generative engine optimization strategy: crawler access, answer-first content, structure, expertise, off-site signals and measurement.
reason: How-to guide supporting the /generative-engine-optimization service page; retargeted to "generative engine optimization strategy" so it doesn't compete with the live "What Is Generative Engine Optimization?" post.
body_html:
A generative engine optimization strategy is a step-by-step plan for getting your content found, understood and cited by AI search tools such as Google's AI Overviews, AI Mode and ChatGPT search. It starts with crawler access, then answer-first content, clear structure, real expertise, off-site reputation and a way to measure citations.

GEO in brief

Generative engine optimization (GEO) is the work of becoming a source that AI search tools quote, mention or link when they write an answer. The term comes from a research paper, "GEO: Generative Engine Optimization" by Aggarwal and colleagues, accepted at the KDD 2024 conference. For the full definition and how it relates to labels like AEO and AI SEO, read what generative engine optimization is and how it works; this guide focuses on the steps.

How GEO differs from SEO

Less than the hype suggests. Google's guidance on AI features and your website says there are no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, and no special optimizations necessary. A page needs to be indexed and eligible to show in Search with a snippet. The same SEO fundamentals apply.

What changes is the unit of success. Classic SEO aims for a ranking and a click. GEO aims for inclusion in an answer, which might be a citation, a mention of your brand, or a link the reader may or may not click.

Classic SEO focus

  • Whole pages ranking for a query
  • Clicks and rankings as the main measure
  • Mostly about your own site
  • One main search engine to plan around

What GEO adds

  • Passages that make sense when lifted on their own
  • Citations and brand mentions, with or without a click
  • Your reputation on reviews, directories, forums and other sites
  • Several engines, each with its own crawlers and sources

How AI search engines choose sources

No AI company publishes a full formula, so be skeptical of anyone who claims to know one. What is documented is still useful.

Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode may use a "query fan-out" technique: running several related searches on subtopics to gather supporting pages. That means a page can be cited for a sub-question even if it doesn't rank for the main query. Covering the natural follow-up questions on a topic gives you more chances to be picked.

Other engines rely on their own crawlers. OpenAI's crawler documentation explains that OAI-SearchBot is used to surface websites in ChatGPT search, and recommends allowing it in robots.txt if you want to appear there. It's separate from GPTBot, which collects content that may be used for model training. OpenAI says each setting is independent.

A generative engine optimization strategy in 7 steps

Here's the work in the order I'd tackle it. When I look at a site for AI visibility, I start with step 1 because nothing else matters if the right crawlers are blocked.

  1. Make sure AI crawlers can reach you

    Check robots.txt, your CDN and any firewall or bot-protection settings. Security tools sometimes block crawlers you want. Decide on each bot deliberately: Googlebot for Search (including AI features), OAI-SearchBot for ChatGPT search, and training crawlers like GPTBot or Google-Extended based on your own policy. Then confirm key pages are indexed in Google Search Console and aren't blocked by noindex or nosnippet by mistake.

  2. Put the answer first

    Open each page or section with a direct, one- to three-sentence answer to the question it targets, then add detail, examples and context. Use question-style headings that match how people actually ask.

  3. Structure content so passages stand alone

    Use descriptive headings, short paragraphs and real lists. Avoid sections that only make sense after the one before ("as mentioned above"). Keep important information in text, not only in images, PDFs or widgets; Google's guidance calls this out directly. This is the focus of my content structure work for AI search.

  4. Show real expertise

    Name the author and explain their experience. Add first-hand detail: your process, real examples, what you've seen work and not work. Cite primary sources when you state facts, and keep numbers current.

  5. Use structured data that matches the page

    No special schema is required for AI features, but structured data still helps search engines understand who you are and what a page covers, and Google recommends that it match the visible text. Organization, LocalBusiness, Product, Article and FAQPage markup are common starting points. My schema markup service covers this in detail.

  6. Strengthen your presence beyond your site

    Keep Google Business Profile and Merchant Center details accurate; Google lists both in its AI features guidance. Make your name, address, services and descriptions consistent across directories and social profiles, and earn mentions on reputable industry sites, local news and relevant community discussions.

  7. Keep content fresh

    Review your most important pages on a schedule and update facts, prices, screenshots and dates. Remove or redirect outdated pages that could be quoted with old information.

A robots.txt starting point

Here is an example for a business that wants to appear in Google Search and ChatGPT search but doesn't want its content used to train OpenAI's models. Adjust it to your own policy before using it.

# Example policy only. Search crawlers in, one training crawler out.
User-agent: Googlebot
Allow: /

User-agent: OAI-SearchBot
Allow: /

User-agent: GPTBot
Disallow: /

Watch out Blocking a training crawler and blocking a search crawler are different decisions. Google's AI features page points to snippet controls (nosnippet, data-nosnippet, max-snippet or noindex) for limiting what shows from your pages in Search, and to Google-Extended for limiting AI training and grounding in some of Google's other systems. Blocking Googlebot to "opt out of AI" removes you from regular search too. OpenAI notes robots.txt changes can take about 24 hours to apply to ChatGPT search.

Check where your site stands

Use this self-check before writing new content. The top items carry more weight because they block everything else.

  • Googlebot and OAI-SearchBot are allowed in robots.txt, and your CDN or firewall doesn't block them?
  • Your key service or product pages are indexed in Search Console, without noindex or nosnippet set by mistake?
  • Each key page opens with a direct answer of one to three sentences?
  • Important details (prices, service areas, specs) are in page text, not only in images or PDFs?
  • Your Google Business Profile or Merchant Center details match your website?
  • Pages name an author or business owner with relevant experience?
  • Structured data on key pages matches what's visible on the page?
  • You have a saved list of customer questions you check in AI tools on a schedule?

The foundations are in place. Spend your time on off-site reputation, fresh content and tracking a consistent prompt list.

Some basics are missing. Fix any crawl or indexing gaps first, then rework your top pages so the answer comes first.

Start with access. Check robots.txt, your CDN settings and Search Console indexing before writing anything new.

How to measure your GEO strategy

Measurement is still the weakest part of GEO. Google Search Console counts traffic from AI features in the Performance report under the "Web" search type, together with regular results, so you can't separate it there. A few practical approaches:

  • Prompt tracking. Keep a list of the questions your customers ask, run them in Google, ChatGPT and other tools on a regular schedule, and record whether you're mentioned or cited.
  • Referral traffic in GA4. Visits from AI tools often show up with referrers such as chatgpt.com or perplexity.ai. Group them in a custom channel or exploration.
  • Branded search and direct traffic. People who see your name in an AI answer often search for you later rather than clicking straight through.
  • Leads. Ask new inquiries how they found you, and include AI tools as an option.

A prompt log doesn't need special software. A spreadsheet with these columns is enough to see a trend month to month:

Date | Tool (AI Overviews, AI Mode, ChatGPT, other) | Prompt, word for word
Mentioned? (yes/no) | Linked? (yes/no) | Which page was cited
Competitors or other sources named | Anything wrong about you in the answer

Run the same prompts, worded the same way, each time. AI answers vary between runs, so watch the pattern over months, not one result. For local businesses, the last column matters most: an old address or a dropped service in an AI answer shows which listing or page to fix first.

If you want a quick read on where you stand, my free AI visibility check looks at whether AI tools recommend your business.

Common GEO mistakes to avoid

  • Chasing tricks. Keyword-stuffed "AI-friendly" pages and hidden text for bots can hurt you in regular search, which AI features depend on.
  • Neglecting the basics. Slow, thin or poorly linked pages rarely get cited.
  • Expecting guarantees. No one can promise a citation. Google itself notes that indexing and serving aren't guaranteed.

If you'd like help putting this into practice, I offer generative engine optimization services that start with an audit of how AI tools see your business today. Reach out whenever it suits you.

Is generative engine optimization replacing SEO?

No. GEO depends on SEO. Google's AI features draw on pages that are indexed and eligible for regular search results, and other AI tools rely on crawling and search indexes too. If your pages can't be crawled, rank poorly or say very little, they're unlikely to be cited. Think of GEO as SEO with extra attention on clear answers, quotable passages and your reputation across the web.

Do I need an llms.txt file or special markup for AI search?

Not for Google. Its AI features guidance says you don't need new machine-readable files, AI text files or special schema.org markup to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode. An llms.txt file is a proposed convention some sites use, but adding one is optional. Your time is usually better spent on crawl access, clear content and accurate structured data that matches the page.

How long does generative engine optimization take to work?

There's no fixed timeline. Changes like unblocking a crawler or fixing indexing issues can take effect as soon as pages are recrawled. Content and reputation work usually takes longer, because it depends on search engines reprocessing pages and on other sites mentioning you. Track a consistent set of prompts monthly so you can see whether citations and mentions are trending in the right direction.

Can small and local businesses benefit from GEO?

Yes, often more than large brands expect. People ask AI tools for local recommendations, comparisons and how-to answers. A complete Google Business Profile, consistent directory listings, genuine reviews and service pages that answer real customer questions all give AI tools clear information to work with. Local businesses with a focused niche can be easier to describe accurately than broad national brands.

title: Mobile SEO Platforms: What to Look for in Tools and Software
seo_title: Mobile SEO Platform: What to Look for in Tools
meta_description: What to look for in a mobile SEO platform: smartphone crawling, real-user Core Web Vitals with INP, mobile rank tracking, and clean reporting.
excerpt: No single tool covers all of mobile SEO. Here's what a mobile SEO platform should do and how to choose tools that fit your site and team.
tags: mobile SEO, Core Web Vitals, SEO tools, mobile-first indexing, Search Console
topic: Buyer's guide to the features that matter in mobile SEO tools and software
reason: Commercial-intent post supporting the mobile SEO service page for people comparing mobile SEO tools
body_html:
A mobile SEO platform is any tool, or set of tools, that shows how your site performs for people and search engines on phones: how Google crawls the mobile version, how fast pages load and respond, and where you rank in mobile results. The right one depends on your site's size and how you report.

There's no single product that does everything. Most teams combine free Google tools with one or two paid tools. This post explains what to look for so you can compare options on features that matter instead of on marketing pages.

Why does mobile SEO need its own tools?

Google indexes and ranks the mobile version of your pages. Its documentation on mobile-first indexing best practices says Google uses the mobile version of a site's content, crawled with its smartphone crawler, for indexing and ranking. If something is missing or broken on mobile, Google may not see it, even if the desktop page looks fine.

So the questions you need answered are mobile-specific: does the mobile page have the same main content, headings, structured data and meta tags as desktop? How fast does it load and respond on real phones? Where do you rank when someone searches from a phone, often from a specific location?

Watch out Google retired its Mobile-Friendly Test and Search Console's Mobile Usability report in December 2023, as announced on the Search Central blog, and pointed people to Lighthouse instead. If a vendor or checklist still sends you there, or still reports First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital, it's out of date. That's a quick way to judge how current a tool is.

What should a mobile SEO platform do?

Use this table as your comparison checklist. The last column is what I'd actually do during a free trial, on your own site, before paying for anything.

FeatureWhy it mattersHow to test it in a trial
Crawls as a smartphoneGoogle indexes the mobile version, so the crawler should fetch pages with a smartphone user agent (the label a bot uses to say what device it is) and render JavaScriptCrawl a page whose content loads with scripts and confirm that content and its links show up
Compares mobile and desktopDynamic serving or a separate mobile site can drop text, titles, structured data or robots tags on phonesCrawl both versions of a few key templates and check that the tool flags differences
Real-user Core Web VitalsField data from real visitors is what Search Console reports; lab tests only simulate a visitCheck that it shows LCP, INP and CLS, labels field vs lab data, and splits mobile from desktop
Mobile rank tracking by locationMobile and desktop results can differ, and local results change from one area to the nextSet one keyword to mobile in your town and confirm you can pick both device and location
Search Console and GA4 connectionsSearch Console is Google's own data on clicks, impressions and indexing; GA4 shows what visitors do after they landConnect both and confirm the numbers match what you see in Google's own interfaces
Prioritized issuesLong warning lists don't help on their ownLook for grouping by template, a count of affected pages, and a way to mark issues fixed
Fits your size and teamA ten-page local site and a large store need different limitsCheck crawl limits, tracked keywords, user seats and scheduled crawls against your real numbers

The Core Web Vitals numbers a tool should report

Core Web Vitals are Google's three page experience measurements. INP replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. Google's Core Web Vitals report in Search Console uses real-user data, reports mobile and desktop separately, and lists these thresholds for "good":

2.5 sLargest Contentful Paint, loading (Search Console Help)

200 msInteraction to Next Paint, responsiveness (Search Console Help)

0.1Cumulative Layout Shift, visual stability (Search Console Help)

If a tool's "pass" doesn't line up with those numbers, ask the vendor what it's measuring. If you'd rather not manage rank tracking yourself, see my keyword tracking service.

Which tools make up a typical mobile SEO platform?

Tool typeExamplesWhat it answers
Google's free toolsSearch Console, PageSpeed Insights, Lighthouse in Chrome DevToolsHow Google sees your pages, real-user Core Web Vitals, lab performance audits
Site crawlersScreaming Frog, SitebulbTechnical issues across every page, mobile rendering, structured data
SEO suitesSemrush, AhrefsMobile rankings, competitors, site audits, keyword research
ReportingData Studio (formerly Looker Studio), GA4Combined dashboards and what visitors do after they land

These are examples, not endorsements. Feature sets change often, so confirm current capabilities in each tool's documentation or a free trial before you commit.

How do you choose the right mobile SEO platform?

Free Google tools are enough when

  • Your site has a few dozen pages and one main template
  • The site is fully responsive, with no separate mobile version
  • Search Console shows no Core Web Vitals or indexing problems
  • You serve one area and can check rankings by hand

Add a crawler or rank tracker when

  • You have more pages or templates than you can check by hand
  • Content is loaded by JavaScript or differs on phones
  • Search Console flags issues and you need to find which pages cause them
  • You report mobile rankings across several towns or clients

Score your own situation below. It weighs the same signals, so the result tells you which side you're closer to.

  • Your site has more than about 100 pages, or several page templates?
  • Search Console shows mobile URLs as "Poor" or "Need improvement" in the Core Web Vitals report?
  • Some content or links only appear after JavaScript runs, or your mobile site differs from desktop?
  • You need mobile rankings for more than one town or service area?
  • Someone other than you needs a regular report on mobile performance?

A crawler, a rank tracker or both will likely save you time. Shortlist two and test them on your own site.

Start with Search Console and PageSpeed Insights, and add one paid tool for the specific gap you scored on.

Google's free tools probably cover you for now. Check Search Console monthly and revisit this when the site grows.

Whichever way you go, plan who will act on the findings. A tool finds problems; someone still has to fix templates, images and scripts.

Get help choosing and using the right tools

If you'd rather have someone audit your mobile setup and fix what matters most, see how my mobile SEO services work. For deeper crawl and indexing problems, my technical SEO services pick up where tools leave off.

Is Google Search Console enough for mobile SEO?

For small sites, it covers a lot: indexing, real-user Core Web Vitals, and search performance you can filter by device. What it doesn't do is crawl every page on demand, compare mobile and desktop versions side by side, or track rankings by location. Most growing sites add a crawler and a rank tracker once Search Console points to problems worth investigating.

Do you still need to test mobile usability now that Google's test is gone?

Yes. The tool was retired, not the need. Use Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools for lab checks, test key pages on real phones, and watch Search Console's Core Web Vitals report for real-user data. Pay attention to tap targets, text size, pop-ups that cover content, and forms that are hard to complete on a small screen.

How often should you run mobile SEO checks?

Check Search Console weekly or monthly, depending on how often your site changes. Run a full crawl after any redesign, migration, theme update, or new plugin, since those are common times for mobile issues to appear. Core Web Vitals data in Search Console is based on real visits over time, so give changes a few weeks before judging results.

title: Landing Page Optimization Checklist: 15 Fixes That Lift Conversions
meta_description: A landing page optimization checklist with 15 practical fixes for message, trust, forms, speed and testing, so more visitors call, book or buy.
excerpt: Fifteen practical landing page fixes, from matching the headline to the click to passing Core Web Vitals, so more of your visitors take the next step.
tags: landing pages, conversion rate optimization, Core Web Vitals, Google Ads, forms
topic: A 15-point landing page optimization checklist covering message, trust, forms, speed and testing.
reason: New guide to support the /seo-services/landing-page-optimization service page for the keyword "landing page optimization".
body_html:
Landing page optimization is the process of improving a single page so more of the people who arrive on it take the action you want, like calling, booking or buying. The fixes that matter most are matching the visitor's intent, a clear offer, fast loading, an easy form and visible trust signals.

What landing page optimization means

A landing page is any page someone lands on from an ad, a search result, an email or a social post. Some are built for one campaign. Others are service pages or product pages that happen to get a lot of traffic. Either way, the page has one job: get the visitor to take the next step.

Optimizing it means finding what stops people from taking that step and removing it. Sometimes that's the message. Sometimes it's speed, a confusing form, or a page that looks fine on a laptop and falls apart on a phone.

It matters for paid and organic traffic alike. Google Ads uses a measure called landing page experience to estimate how relevant and useful your page will be to people who click your ad. For SEO, a page that answers the search clearly and works well on mobile gives searchers what they came for.

How do you know which landing pages to fix first?

Start with pages that get meaningful traffic but convert poorly, then watch how people actually use them.

  1. Rank pages by traffic and conversions

    In GA4, compare sessions and key events (conversions) by landing page. A page with lots of sessions and a low conversion rate is a better first target than a page that converts well but gets little traffic.

  2. Check the ad side

    In Google Ads, check the landing pages report and the landing page experience status on your keywords. Keywords marked "below average" point to pages worth reviewing.

  3. Check the search side

    In Search Console, look for pages with plenty of impressions but few clicks. That often points to a title or snippet that doesn't match the search.

  4. Watch real behavior

    Heatmaps and session recordings show where people stop scrolling, what they tap on, and where they give up on a form.

Before you change anything, it helps to know what a fix could be worth. Here's the simple math, using your own numbers in place of the example defaults:

Monthly visits to the page

Current conversion rate (%)

Conversion rate you're aiming for (%)

About {} extra calls, bookings or sales a month

Run it for your two or three busiest pages. The one with the biggest gap is usually where to start, even if it isn't the page you like least.

The landing page optimization checklist: 15 fixes

Work through these in order; tick them off as you go, and the detail for each is below. The early fixes tend to matter most, and they don't need a redesign.

  • Match the headline to the click
  • State the offer in one sentence
  • Give each page one main goal
  • Write calls to action that describe the result
  • Answer the main objections on the page
  • Show real proof near the call to action
  • Make it obvious who you are
  • Use real photos where you can
  • Cut form fields to what you actually need
  • Make the form work well on a phone
  • Confirm what happens next
  • Get Core Web Vitals into the "good" range
  • Design for mobile first
  • Keep the page scannable
  • Test one meaningful change at a time

1. Match the headline to the click

If someone clicked an ad for "emergency furnace repair," the headline should say emergency furnace repair, not "Welcome to Smith Heating." The faster visitors confirm they're in the right place, the more likely they are to stay. To check, put each ad or top search query next to the headline it lands on. If the main words don't appear in the headline, that's your first fix.

2. State the offer in one sentence

Right under the headline, say what you do, who it's for and what happens next. Skip the slogan. A pattern you can adapt:

[What you do] for [who] in [area]. [What happens when they reach out], usually within [timeframe].

Example: Furnace and boiler repair for homes in Albany and Saratoga County. Call or book online and a technician will confirm a visit time, usually the same day.

Only promise a timeframe you actually meet.

3. Give each page one main goal

A page that asks visitors to call, subscribe, download and follow you on social media splits their attention. Pick the action that matters most and make everything else secondary.

4. Write calls to action that describe the result

"Get my free quote" or "Book a 15-minute call" tells people what they'll get. "Submit" doesn't.

5. Answer the main objections on the page

Price range, service area, timing, what's included, what happens after they reach out. If visitors have to leave the page to find answers, many won't come back. The questions customers ask on the phone are the best source for this section.

6. Show real proof near the call to action

Genuine reviews, recognizable client logos, certifications, licenses or warranties. Put them where people are deciding, not only at the bottom.

7. Make it obvious who you are

Your business name, location or service area, and a real way to contact you. A phone number that's tappable on mobile is a simple win for local businesses.

8. Use real photos where you can

Your team, your work, your location. Generic stock photos rarely build trust.

9. Cut form fields to what you actually need

Every extra field is another reason to quit. If you only need a name, email and a short message to follow up, stop there. A useful test: for each field, ask what you do with the answer before the first call. If the answer is "nothing," remove it. My form optimization service focuses on exactly this.

10. Make the form work well on a phone

Use the right input types so the correct keyboard appears, keep labels visible, and show clear error messages next to the field that needs fixing.

11. Confirm what happens next

After someone submits, tell them when they'll hear back and what to expect. It reduces anxiety and repeat submissions.

12. Get Core Web Vitals into the "good" range

Google's web.dev guidance sets these "good" thresholds, measured at the 75th percentile of page views:

2.5 sLargest Contentful Paint: how fast the main content appears (web.dev)

200 msInteraction to Next Paint: how quickly the page responds to taps and clicks (web.dev)

0.1Cumulative Layout Shift: how much the layout jumps around (web.dev)

The 75th percentile means most of your visits, including slower phones and connections, need to hit the target, not just your own fast laptop. Compressed images, fewer third-party scripts and lighter page builders usually help most. My page speed optimization work covers this.

13. Design for mobile first

Check the page on an actual phone. The headline, offer and call to action should be visible without much scrolling, buttons should be easy to tap, and pop-ups shouldn't cover the content.

14. Keep the page scannable

Short paragraphs, descriptive subheadings and bullet lists help people find the part they care about. Most visitors skim before they read.

15. Test one meaningful change at a time

Once the basics are in place, A/B test the elements most likely to change behavior: the headline, the offer, the form or the call to action. Let tests run long enough to collect a reliable sample before deciding. My A/B testing service handles setup and analysis.

Watch out Small-business pages often don't get enough conversions for an A/B test to give a clear answer in a reasonable time. If your page gets a handful of leads a month, make the fixes in this list directly, note the date, and compare the following months instead. Save formal tests for pages with steady traffic.

How landing page optimization affects SEO and Google Ads

For SEO, the same fixes that help visitors convert also help a page serve the search well: a clear answer to the query, a fast and stable mobile experience, and content organized under descriptive headings. Core Web Vitals are part of how Google evaluates page experience.

For Google Ads, landing page experience is one of the factors Google uses when judging ad quality, alongside expected click-through rate and ad relevance. Keywords marked "below average" for landing page experience are a signal to review the page those ads send people to.

The overlap is the useful part. One well-built page can support both channels, so you don't need a separate page for every campaign unless the message genuinely differs.

Next steps

If you'd like a second set of eyes on your most important pages, I offer landing page optimization services that start with a review of how your current pages perform. Get in touch whenever it's useful.

Is landing page optimization the same as conversion rate optimization?

They overlap, but landing page optimization is narrower. It focuses on individual pages where visitors arrive, usually from ads or search. Conversion rate optimization (CRO) looks at the whole path to a sale or lead, including navigation, checkout, pricing pages and follow-up. Most CRO programs start with landing pages because that's where improvements are easiest to measure and affect the most traffic.

How long should a landing page be?

As long as it needs to be to answer the visitor's questions, and no longer. A simple, low-commitment offer like a free consultation can work with a short page. A larger purchase or an unfamiliar service usually needs more detail, proof and answers to objections. Watch scroll depth and where people drop off rather than aiming for a set word count.

What tools help with landing page optimization?

You can do a lot with free tools. GA4 shows traffic and key events by landing page. Search Console shows which searches lead to each page. PageSpeed Insights reports Core Web Vitals from real users and lab tests. Heatmap and session recording tools show how people actually use the page, and an A/B testing tool lets you compare versions with real traffic.

How often should I review my landing pages?

Check your highest-traffic pages monthly for conversion rate, speed and any broken forms or links. Review them in more depth whenever you change an ad campaign, an offer or your pricing, since the page needs to match. A quarterly pass through the full checklist is a sensible rhythm for most small businesses, with A/B tests running in between when traffic allows.

title: Large-Scale SEO Playbook: Managing Thousands of Pages
seo_title: Large Scale SEO Playbook for Sites With Thousands of Pages
meta_description: A large scale SEO playbook for thousands of pages: page inventories, crawl budget, filter URLs, template fixes, sitemaps, and monitoring by page type.
excerpt: When a site has thousands of pages, you fix templates, not pages. This playbook covers page inventories, crawl budget, faceted navigation, sitemaps, internal linking, and monitoring.
tags: enterprise SEO, technical SEO, crawl budget, faceted navigation, XML sitemaps
topic: How to manage SEO for sites with thousands of pages through templates, crawl control, sitemaps, and page-type monitoring.
reason: New guide supporting the Enterprise SEO service page (/seo-services/enterprise-seo) for the keyword large scale seo.
body_html:
Large scale SEO is the work of keeping thousands of pages crawlable, indexable, and useful without fixing them one by one. You manage templates instead of pages, control which URLs search engines spend time on, and monitor results by page type so problems show up before traffic drops.

What changes when a site gets big

On a 30-page site, you can open every page and fix what you find. On a site with 20,000 product, location, or article pages, that stops working. A few things change:

  • Templates multiply everything. One bad canonical tag in a product template is thousands of bad canonical tags.
  • URLs multiply on their own. Filters, sort orders, tracking parameters, and internal search can create far more URLs than you have real pages.
  • Google won't crawl everything right away. It decides how much of your site to crawl and how often.
  • More people touch the site. Developers, merchandisers, and content teams all ship changes that affect SEO.

The playbook below runs in this order. Each stage depends on the one before it, so resist the urge to start with sitemaps or content.

  1. InventoryGroup every URL into page types
  2. Crawl controlDecide what Google should and shouldn't fetch

Start with a page inventory

Before fixing anything, group every URL on the site into page types and decide what each type is for. A crawl export, your XML sitemaps, and Search Console data together give you the full list.

Page typeShould it be indexed?What to decide
Product or service detailUsually yesHow to handle out-of-stock or discontinued items
Category or hubYesWhich categories deserve unique copy
Filtered or sorted listingsOnly someWhich filter combinations match real searches
Internal search resultsUsually noHow to keep them from being crawled
Location pagesYes, if uniqueWhat makes each one more than a name swap

For each page type, note roughly how many URLs it has, which template builds it, and who owns that template. This becomes the map for everything else.

The quickest red flag in an inventory is a gap between three numbers: pages you meant to have, URLs your crawler found, and URLs in your sitemaps. Example: if you sell 4,000 products but a crawl finds 60,000 URLs, the extra 56,000 are almost always filters, sort orders or parameters, and that's where to look first.

Large scale SEO starts with crawl budget

Crawl budget is the number of URLs Google can and wants to crawl on your site. Google's guide to optimizing your crawl budget explains it as two parts: a crawl capacity limit (how much your server can handle) and crawl demand (how much Google wants to crawl, based on things like popularity and how often pages change). The guide is aimed at sites like these, which Google calls rough estimates:

1M+ pageswith content that changes about weekly (Google crawl budget guide)

10,000+ pageswith content that changes daily (Google crawl budget guide)

It also applies to sites with many URLs stuck at "Discovered - currently not indexed" in Search Console. Even below those numbers, the same habits keep crawling focused on pages that matter:

  • Consolidate duplicate content so Google isn't crawling the same thing at many addresses.
  • Use robots.txt to block URLs you never want crawled, such as internal search results.
  • Return a 404 or 410 status for pages that are permanently gone.
  • Fix soft 404s, where an empty or "not found" page returns a success code.
  • Avoid long redirect chains.
  • Keep sitemaps current, with accurate lastmod dates.
  • Keep server response times fast and stable.

Watch out The same guide advises against using noindex to save crawl budget. Google still has to request the page to see the tag, so the crawl happens anyway. If the goal is fewer crawled URLs, use robots.txt; if the goal is keeping a page out of results, use noindex. Don't combine them on the same URL: Google's noindex documentation notes that if robots.txt blocks a page, the crawler never sees its noindex rule.

Control filters and URL parameters

Faceted navigation, the filters for size, color, price, or location, is the most common source of runaway URLs. Google's guide to managing faceted navigation URLs splits the decision in two.

If filtered pages don't need to rank

  • Block their parameters in robots.txt
  • Or put filters after a # in the URL, which Google generally ignores for crawling and indexing
  • Canonical tags and nofollow on filter links can help, but Google notes they're usually less effective over time than robots.txt

If some filtered pages should rank

  • Use standard & separators between parameters
  • Keep filters in a consistent order, with no duplicate filters
  • Return a 404 for combinations with no results
  • Give the combinations people search for their own indexable pages

Google's guide includes this robots.txt example for blocking filter parameters while still allowing an unfiltered listing. Swap in your own parameter names, and test the rules before you ship them:

user-agent: Googlebot
disallow: /*?*products=
disallow: /*?*color=
disallow: /*?*size=
allow: /*?products=all$

To decide which combinations deserve their own pages, use keyword research. My rule: if a combination like "red running shoes" has its own search demand and enough products to fill a page, it's a candidate. If it only exists because the filter does, block it.

Fix problems at the template level

At scale, every page-level fix should be a template fix. Before each release, crawl a sample of every main template on staging and tick through this list:

  • Title tags and meta descriptions are built from unique fields (product name, location, category), not one repeated line
  • Indexable pages have a self-referencing canonical tag
  • Structured data matches what's visible on the page
  • Breadcrumbs and related-item links point to other indexable pages
  • Empty states make sense: what an out-of-stock product or a zero-result category shows and which status code it returns
  • Pagination uses normal links Google can follow
  • The staging noindex setting is not in the release going live

Build a sitemap system, not a single sitemap

Google's sitemap documentation limits each sitemap to 50,000 URLs or 50MB uncompressed, and lets you group several sitemaps under one sitemap index file. Split sitemaps by page type (products, categories, locations, articles). Then the Page indexing report in Search Console can be filtered by sitemap, so you can see indexing for each page type separately. Generate sitemaps automatically, include only canonical, indexable pages, and update lastmod only when a page meaningfully changes.

To plan the files for one page type, divide its URL count by the 50,000 limit and round up. The calculator does that for you; the default is only an example.

Plan internal linking on purpose

On a big site, internal links decide which pages Google finds and how often it returns. Keep important pages within a few clicks of the homepage through category and hub pages. Use breadcrumbs, "related" modules, and links from popular articles to deeper pages. Check your crawl for orphan pages that appear in sitemaps but have no internal links pointing to them.

Site-wide totals hide problems. A sharp drop in one template can look like a small dip when it's averaged across the whole site.

Scheduled crawls

A weekly or monthly crawl with alerts for spikes in 404s, 5xx errors, new noindex tags, or canonical changes.

Work with your dev and content teams

Most large-site SEO problems come from ordinary releases. Add SEO checks to the definition of done for tickets that touch templates, URLs, or navigation. Keep a simple change log with the date and what shipped, so when traffic moves you can match it to a release instead of guessing.

How many pages make a site "large" for SEO?

There's no official cutoff. Google's crawl budget guide uses rough markers, about a million pages that change weekly or 10,000 pages that change daily, for when crawl budget needs active management. In practice, the approach in this guide starts paying off once you have more pages than you can review by hand, usually in the low thousands, or once filters and parameters start generating URLs nobody planned.

Should you noindex thin pages or remove them?

It depends on whether the page helps visitors. If people use it but it shouldn't appear in search, such as a filtered view, noindex or blocking the parameter in robots.txt can work. If the page has no purpose, remove it and return a 404 or 410, or redirect it to the closest relevant page. Improving thin pages with real, unique content is often the better option for pages that match a genuine search.

How do you see what Googlebot is crawling?

Start with the Crawl Stats report under Settings in Search Console. It shows total crawl requests, response codes, file types, and how quickly your server responds. For page-level detail, look at your server logs and filter for verified Googlebot requests. Logs show exactly which URLs get crawled, so you can spot time spent on parameters, redirects, or pages you thought were blocked.
